1. Market Overview & Long-Term Price Trend

Gold's price trajectory from August 2000 to March 2026 is one of the defining macro-asset narratives of the early 21st century. Over this ~25.5-year window, gold compounded at 12.4% annually, transforming from approximately $274 per ounce to $5377 — a roughly 19.6× total appreciation.

The all-time high of $5,377 was reached on 03 March 2026. Notable phases include:

  • 2000–2008 Secular Bull: Gold rose from ~$274 to ~$870, driven by USD weakness, the post-dot-com easing cycle, and early signs of financial stress. The 2008 crisis provided an acceleration point as safe-haven flows intensified.
  • 2008–2011 Crisis Rally & Peak: Zero interest-rate policy (ZIRP), quantitative easing, and sovereign debt fears propelled gold to its then-record near $1,900 in September 2011.
  • 2011–2015 Mean Reversion / Bear Market: Taper tantrums and a strengthening dollar drove gold down ~45% from peak to trough, bottoming near $1,050 in late 2015.
  • 2016–2019 Recovery: A gradual recovery amid geopolitical uncertainty and renewed dovish central bank posture.
  • 2020–2025 Acceleration: Pandemic-era stimulus, persistent inflation, central bank buying, and geopolitical fragmentation have driven gold above $5,000 — a multi-year acceleration well beyond prior trend rates.
🔖The maximum drawdown of 44.4% occurred during the 2011–2015 bear phase, representing a significant stress test for gold allocations. The current regime shows gold trading near all-time highs with drawdowns contained below ~10% over the past 3 years.

2. Volatility Analysis & Regime Detection

Volatility regime detection is a critical input for position sizing, risk budgeting, and option-strategy design. We classify each trading day into one of four regimes — low, normal, elevated, and extreme — based on the 63-trading-day (~3-month) rolling annualized volatility relative to its full-sample percentile distribution.

Volatility Cone by Lookback Window

The volatility cone shows the range of realized annualized volatility across different rolling-window lengths (5 to 252 trading days). This reveals the term structure of volatility and whether short-term vol tends to overshoot or undershoot long-term vol.

ⓘThe median volatility is relatively stable across window lengths (13–16% annualized), confirming that gold volatility is not strongly term-structure-dependent. The wide max-min spread at short windows (5–21 days) reflects episodic vol spikes that mean-revert quickly.

4. Return Distribution & Tail Risk

The distribution of gold's daily log returns reveals important risk characteristics — particularly the fat-tail behavior that standard mean-variance frameworks underestimate.

Tail Risk Metrics

MetricValueInterpretation
VaR (95%)-1.76%Daily loss exceeded only 5% of the time
VaR (99%)-3.10%Daily loss exceeded only 1% of the time
CVaR (95%)-2.64%Average loss in the worst 5% of days
CVaR (99%)-4.27%Average loss in the worst 1% of days
🔖Gold's daily returns exhibit negatively skewed behavior (skewness = -0.47) with extremely heavy-tailed behavior (excess kurtosis = 7.0). The Jarque-Bera test emphatically rejects normality (p ≈ 0.0e+00). The QQ plot shows pronounced deviations from the normal reference line in both tails. The CVaR at 99% (-4.27%) indicates that, conditional on being in the worst 1% of days, the average loss is approximately 4.3× the daily standard deviation — a clear manifestation of tail risk.

5. Momentum Dynamics & Liquidity Behavior

Moving Average Crossovers

The 50/200-day SMA crossover is a canonical trend-following signal. The chart below overlays both moving averages on the price series, with a signal ribbon indicating periods when the 50-day SMA exceeds the 200-day SMA (bullish trend) versus when it falls below (bearish trend).

Key observations from the SMA crossover system:

  • Gold has spent the majority of the post-2001 period in a "golden cross" state (SMA 50 > SMA 200), consistent with its secular bull market.
  • The 2013–2018 period saw extended "death cross" conditions, corresponding to the post-taper bear market.
  • The current regime is firmly bullish with SMA 50 well above SMA 200 since mid-2019, interrupted only briefly in 2022.

Rate-of-Change Momentum

Multi-horizon rate-of-change (ROC) measures reveal the speed and persistence of price trends. The chart below shows 1-month, 3-month, and 12-month ROCs.

ⓘThe 12-month ROC provides the cleanest trend signal, with sustained positive readings during bull phases and negative readings during bears. The 1-month and 3-month ROCs are noisier but useful for detecting acceleration or deceleration within the prevailing trend.

6. Key Takeaways & Forward-Looking Considerations

Summary of Findings

  1. Secular Bull with Punctuated Bears: Gold's 25-year CAGR of 12.4% masks significant cyclicality — including a ~45% peak-to-trough drawdown (2011–2015). Long-term allocations have been rewarded, but entry timing matters substantially.
  2. Volatility Is Regime-Dependent and Clustered: Four distinct volatility regimes are identifiable. Crisis episodes (2008, 2020) produce extreme vol clustering, but these episodes are relatively short-lived. Current vol (36.5% annualized) is in the extreme regime.
  3. Tail Risk Is Real: With excess kurtosis of 7.0, gold is not normally distributed. The 99% CVaR of -4.27% daily implies that tail-risk hedging (e.g., put options, volatility targeting) adds value for risk-conscious portfolios.
  4. Seasonal Effects Are Subtle: While certain months (notably January) show above-average returns, the statistical evidence for reliable seasonality is weak. Seasonal timing should be a secondary consideration at most.
  5. Momentum Works — Until It Doesn't: Trend-following signals (SMA crossovers, ROC) have historically captured the bulk of gold's secular uptrend while sidestepping major drawdowns. However, whipsaws around turning points (2013, 2022) demonstrate that no signal is infallible.
  6. Volume Confirms Trend Strength: Post-2003 volume data shows a weak correlation with absolute returns, consistent with volume confirming trend strength during directional moves.
